frus-1861-d5:
Writing to Norman Judd on 22 March 1861, William H. Seward set out early orders for Lincoln's new envoy. Judd was the new American minister to Prussia, bound for Berlin. The letter is document 5 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

March 1861 was a month of fresh starts and deep dread. Lincoln's men took posts abroad while the South formed its own government. Seward's early letters to his ministers set the tone each man would take at his court, and this one belongs to that first round. Judd had backed Lincoln for years, and Seward knew he could trust the man's reports from Berlin.
frus-1862-d5:
By the date of 13 December 1861, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 5 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the close of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d5:
Charles Francis Adams dated this dispatch 20 November 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. He was the American minister in London, in post since the spring of 1861. The letter is document 5 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A minister's weekly mail mixed hard news with the feel of a place. Adams sent both: what the British cabinet did, and what London thought of the war's course. Seward read these letters to judge how close Britain stood to a step that could aid the South. This dispatch is one bead on that long string, valued now as part of the whole.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d5: Marshal Stalin answered President Roosevelt on May 26, 1943, in a message kept as Document 5 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The exchange belongs to the months when the two leaders, allies by need who had never met, were feeling their way toward a summit. No topic is named in the catalog record. The message survives in the State Department's Foreign Relations series, where it can be read in the run of their spring correspondence.
frus-1944-quebec-d5:
After a spring gap in the printed record, Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on May 25, 1944. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume's pre-conference correspondence.

Late May 1944 was the invasion's eve: the Normandy armada was loading, Rome was about to fall, and the alliance's attention was fixed on France. A Churchill message in that week belongs to the final alignment of the Western effort before D-Day. For readers, the letter shows the correspondence resuming at full importance just as the war in the West reached its climax, with Quebec's autumn agenda already forming behind it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d5:
J. Edgar Hoover, director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, wrote to Attorney General Tom Clark on 29 August 1945. Hoover guarded the FBI's turf with famous care. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Any plan for a central intelligence agency touched the FBI's work, above all in Latin America, where Hoover's agents had run wartime operations. His letter to his own cabinet chief opens the FBI's thread in the volume. Readers can watch Hoover stake his claims early and in writing. The turf fights that follow in these pages start from positions set down in weeks like this one. They pitted the FBI and the military services against the new central group.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d5: Five days after Stalin's reply, Roosevelt wrote back to the Soviet leader on 27 July 1944. Document 5 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta keeps the exchange in sequence, as the Office of the Historian arranged it. Read together, these short summer messages show the steady written traffic that held the Grand Alliance together between summit meetings.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d5:
Truman held his line on May 11, 1945: Stalin should propose the meeting. He told Churchill it was worth trying, through their ambassadors, to induce Stalin to issue the call. If the effort failed, they could then consider inviting jointly or severally. He added a point of optics for any meeting arranged.

To avoid any suspicion of ganging up, the two Western leaders should travel to the meeting place separately. After the conference, if duties allowed, Truman would gladly visit England, where they could discuss common interests fully. He closed in agreement: the next few months would decide questions of the greatest consequence to the whole world.
frus-1950-55intel-d5: An editorial note in the intelligence community volume points readers to NSC 68. That paper, dated April 14, 1950, is printed in the 1950 volume I at pages 234-292. The Council adopted it on April 25, but President Truman approved it only on September 30. The note sums up its call for a sharp rise in defense spending. Covert action against the Soviet Union and its satellites stood out. Later papers in the series are flagged for readers.
frus-1955-57v16-d5:
Prime Minister Eden wrote to President Eisenhower on July 27, 1956, the day after Egypt seized the Suez Canal Company. Britain and its chiefs of staff, he says, agree that Nasser must not keep control. A firm stand now would hold the maritime powers together.

Oil for Western Europe flows through the canal, and British stocks would last six weeks. Eden argues for an international trust to run it. Force must be ready as a last resort, and staff plans were ordered. He asks for a three-power meeting at once, with France, in London or Washington.
tob-0038-d5:
Volume VI of the Church Committee hearings prints the public examination of the FBI, held by the Senate committee in the mid-1970s. Witnesses from the Bureau and beyond testified on the record. The hearings put domestic intelligence on live public trial.

Testimony and exhibits cover COINTELPRO, the surveillance of Martin Luther King Jr., break-ins, and the Bureau's files on lawful political groups. Senators press officials on who ordered what, and on what law. Read as transcript, the volume lets the public hear the inquiry as it happened, question by question, in the committee's own record.
tob-0039-d5:
Roll 6 of the microfilm set holds another stretch of the Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg, the 1946 to 1947 case against physicians of the Third Reich. The accused faced counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity. The proceedings were taken down verbatim and later filmed.

Sessions on this roll advance the slow contest over camp experiments and the men who ordered, ran, or excused them. Affidavits are challenged, witnesses examined, and papers entered as proof. The trial as a whole helped fix a lasting rule: no medical test on a person without that person's free consent. This roll is one piece of the record from which that rule grew.
